recoveryRoadmap.description: Step-by-step survival and recovery plan for family members when the primary earner is incapacitated or deceased. Follow the phases in order and focus on the first 7 days before moving on.

intro.condolence: We're sorry for your loss. You don't need to do everything at once — this guide shows what matters first.
intro.howToUse: Read the phases in order. Start with the first 7 days, then move into claims, legal settlement and long-term protection.

startHere.0: Get the death certificate and keep at least 15 certified copies.
startHere.1: List all bank accounts, lockers, insurances, loans and pension accounts.
startHere.2: Pause or stop auto-debits and standing instructions.
startHere.3: Tell the employer, insurer and bank about the death, and ask about nominations.
startHere.4: Gather original documents, ID proofs and policy papers in one safe place.
startHere.5: Check whether there is a Will, nominee, or joint holder on each asset.
startHere.6: Keep a simple log of every call, claim or appointment.

legalFramework.2: Insurance Act, 1938 and IRDAI (Policyholder Protection and Grievance Redressal) Regulations, 2024
legalFramework.4: Income Tax Act, 2025 (for returns and legal representative obligations). Old section numbers apply only to years before 1 April 2026.

0.title: Immediate survival
0.focus: Get cash, documents and notices in order

0.action: Get the death certificate and at least 15 certified copies. Apply at the municipal authority or registrar in the place of death.
0.why: Most claims, banks, insurers and legal steps need a certified death certificate. Missing copies create delays for every process.
0.legalRef: Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969

1.action: If you are the surviving joint holder of an 'Either or Survivor' account, you can keep using it. Inform the bank so the deceased's name is removed. Never use the deceased's debit card, PIN, UPI or net-banking login.
1.why: The surviving joint holder can usually continue using the account after informing the bank. Using the deceased's card, PIN or net banking after death can be treated as unauthorised and cause disputes among heirs.

2.action: List every auto-debit, SIP, EMI, insurance premium and standing instruction. Pause or cancel them before they bounce or attract penalties.
2.why: Bounced EMIs and recurring payments can add charges during an already stressful time.
2.legalRef: Standard banking terms and customer instructions

3.action: Inform every lender. Ask in writing whether the loan has credit life or loan protection insurance and request a hold on EMIs while the claim is processed. Do not stop EMIs without written confirmation.
3.why: Some loans are already insured on death, and stopping EMIs without a written decision can create avoidable disputes. Legal heirs are not personally liable for the deceased's loans beyond the assets they inherit, unless they are a co-borrower or guarantor.

4.action: Tell the deceased's employer within 2 to 3 days and ask about salary arrears, gratuity, group life cover and EDLI claims.
4.why: Employers often hold the records and forms needed for salary, gratuity and life cover claims.
4.legalRef: Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972; EPF & MP Act, 1952

5.action: Notify every insurer, including LIC and private policies. Early notice helps the insurer start processing. The 30-day settlement period starts once all documents are submitted.
5.why: A claim is much easier to process when the insurer has the facts early. This is not a legal deadline for all policies, but it helps keep the claim moving.
5.legalRef: IRDAI policyholder protection and grievance rules

6.action: Apply for a Legal Heir Certificate from the Tehsildar, revenue office or municipal corporation. It usually takes 15 to 30 days and unlocks many claims without a court order.
6.why: This is often the fastest document for bank, employer and pension claims.

7.action: Keep health insurance active if the deceased was the proposer of a family floater policy. Contact the insurer to change the proposer before renewal.
7.why: A family health policy can lapse or be harder to continue if the proposer is not updated in time.

8.action: Collect and secure original documents: property papers, insurance policy bonds, bank records, Aadhaar, PAN, title deeds and the Will. Check lockers, safes and email for e-policies.
8.why: Original documents and policy papers often unlock claims faster than copies alone.
8.legalRef: Document retention and insurer KYC rules

criticalMistakes.0: Getting fewer than 10 death certificate copies. You may need 15 or more across all claims.
criticalMistakes.1: Withdrawing from a joint 'Either or Survivor' account without telling the bank about the death. The bank must update records and remove the deceased's name.
criticalMistakes.2: Paying a deceased person's personal loan immediately without checking whether there is credit life or loan protection insurance.
criticalMistakes.3: Throwing away original insurance policy bonds or thinking a digital copy is enough. A lost policy should not stop a valid claim.
criticalMistakes.4: Sharing OTPs, account details or login information with agents or touts offering to 'expedite' claims. This is fraud.
criticalMistakes.5: Assuming there is no Will. Check email, bank locker and a lawyer's office before concluding the estate is intestate.
criticalMistakes.6: Using the deceased's debit card, PIN or net banking after death. This can be treated as unauthorised and cause disputes among heirs.

0.deadline: Register within 21 days. 21-30 days: late fee. 30 days to 1 year: written permission from the registration authority plus affidavit. After 1 year: Magistrate's order.
0.consequence: Delay creates avoidable legal and administrative hassles.

1.deadline: File within 3 years of death, unless the insurer or policy says otherwise.
1.consequence: Claims beyond the statutory or policy limit may be time-barred.

2.deadline: 30 days from when it becomes payable
2.consequence: The employer must pay interest on delay under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972.

jointAccountRules.either_or_survivor: The surviving joint holder can usually continue operating the account after informing the bank and updating records. No court order is usually needed for this account type.
jointAccountRules.former_or_survivor: If the deceased was a 'Former' holder, the surviving holder may still need to submit the death certificate and update the record.
jointAccountRules.single_holder_account: Single-holder accounts are normally frozen once death is intimated. The nominee can claim in line with the bank's procedure. Without a nominee, the heir may need a Legal Heir Certificate or Succession Certificate.

1.title: Claim and transfer
1.focus: File insurance, pension and bank claims and start transmission

0.action: File the insurance death claim with the insurer. Submit the claimant statement, policy details, death certificate and bank details. Early intimation helps the insurer start processing.
0.why: The 30-day settlement period starts once all documents are submitted. Insurers may also pay interest at bank rate plus 2% per year for each day of delay.
0.legalRef: IRDAI policyholder protection and grievance rules

1.action: File the EPF claims together: Form 20, Form 10D and Form 5IF. EDLI is often missed, and it is a separate benefit from the provident fund itself.
1.why: EDLI is a free insurance benefit that often goes unclaimed. Filing all three forms together prevents delays and missed benefits.

2.action: Initiate transmission for single-holder bank accounts. Submit the transmission request, death certificate, KYC and any required indemnity or surety paperwork.
2.why: With a nominee, the process is usually faster. Without a nominee, the bank may ask for a Legal Heir Certificate or Succession Certificate, depending on the amount and bank rules.

3.action: Close or transfer the PPF account using the prescribed claim form for nominees or legal heirs. Submit the claim form and the supporting ID and death certificate to the bank or post office.
3.why: PPF can be closed on death and the nominee or legal heir can receive the balance and interest. The claim is usually simpler than a full succession process.

4.action: File the demat or share transmission request with the DP or registrar. Submit the death certificate, KYC and the relevant transmission form.
4.why: This keeps securities from sitting in the deceased person's name and prevents further delay in transfer.

5.action: Check mutual funds, NPS, post-office schemes, family pension and other investment records. Use MF Central as a single place for mutual fund transfer and folio checks.
5.why: Many family records are split across insurers, depositories, brokers and post offices. This is where missing records often show up.
5.legalRef: AMC, NSDL, CDSL and post office rules

6.action: Apply for a Succession Certificate if there is no nominee and the assets are above the bank or securities threshold. Start early because the process can take months.
6.why: This is often needed for bank balances, securities and other assets without a nominee. A registered Will may still simplify property and title transfer.

7.action: If the family has a bank locker in a sole name, ask the bank for the nominee or legal heir process needed to access the locker and its contents.
7.why: Locker access is often tied to the nominee or legal heir process and the bank's document requirements.

criticalMistakes.0: Filing only EPF withdrawal and missing EDLI. EDLI is often missed, even though it is a free benefit.
criticalMistakes.1: Assuming the bank will automatically transfer the fixed deposit. Each account or deposit must usually be claimed or transmitted separately.
criticalMistakes.2: Not filing the insurance claim because the original policy bond is lost. Insurers usually accept a duplicate or an indemnity arrangement if the policy is valid.
criticalMistakes.3: Ignoring employer records or email trails for group insurance, term cover or salary arrears.
criticalMistakes.4: Signing indemnity bonds or NOC papers without reading them carefully. A lawyer can help if the documents are complex.
criticalMistakes.5: Taking a long time to start the succession process when there is no nominee. The delay creates more disputes and costs.

0.deadline: 30 days from receipt of all documents, unless there is a valid investigation or claim issue.
0.consequence: The insurer may need to pay interest or the claim may be escalated through the grievance channel.

1.consequence: Use the grievance mechanism if the claim is delayed.

2.deadline: 30 days from when it becomes payable
2.consequence: The employer must pay interest on delay under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972.

1.epfClaimNote: EPFO can process claims with fewer document issues than many families expect. Minor children usually do not need a guardianship certificate for EPF claims to be credited to the child’s account.
1.personalLawNote: The Hindu Succession Act applies to Hindus, Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists. Muslims follow personal law; a Will can cover up to one-third of assets. Christians and Parsis follow the Indian Succession Act. Goa follows the Goa Civil Code. You should seek legal help for state-specific or personal-law issues.

2.title: Legal and financial settlement
2.focus: Mutate property records, complete tax filing and resolve debt and title issues

0.action: File the deceased's final Income Tax Return as the Legal Representative. Register as the Legal Representative on the income tax portal before filing.
0.why: The legal representative may be liable for outstanding taxes and penalties. Missing the final return can create avoidable problems.
0.legalRef: Income Tax Act, 2025; prior year section references apply only before 1 April 2026

1.action: Start property mutation at the talathi, tehsildar or municipal corporation. This updates government records, but it is not the same as property transfer.
1.why: Property tax keeps accruing in the deceased's name until mutation. This step is often needed before any sale or mortgage.
1.legalRef: State revenue records and property law

2.action: Check every loan for credit life or loan protection insurance before paying a single EMI. Ask the lender in writing whether the cover is active and paid.
2.why: If a policy exists, the debt may already be covered and there is no need to pay from personal funds without checking first.

3.action: File for Probate of Will if needed. Probate is mandatory in Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai, and it is often recommended elsewhere to reduce disputes.
3.why: A valid Will is easier to administer when title and transfer questions are reduced. Probate can also help clear doubts about authenticity and inheritance.

4.action: Transfer utility connections, such as electricity, gas, water, phone and broadband, to the surviving member using the death certificate and ID proof.
4.why: Utilities in the deceased's name can be difficult to modify and may be disconnected if ownership is unclear.

5.action: Transfer the vehicle registration and insurance to the legal heir or buyer. Inform the RTO within 30 days and apply for transfer within 3 months.
5.why: Keeping the RC or insurance in the deceased's name creates legal and insurance issues. Transfer the motor insurance along with the RC.
5.legalRef: Motor Vehicles Act and RTO rules

6.action: Either equalise or document the estate, including credit cards, personal loans and other liabilities. Heirs are not personally liable beyond the estate unless they are a co-borrower or guarantor.
6.why: Do not pay from your own money before checking the estate and debt position. This prevents unnecessary personal losses and disputes.

1.deadline: No statutory deadline, but file early to reduce disputes and delay.

minorChildrenRights.inheritance: Minor children are class I heirs in many family law contexts and inherit equally with the spouse where applicable.
minorChildrenRights.guardian: The mother is often the natural guardian in a family context, but each case depends on law, facts and any court orders.
minorChildrenRights.restriction: A natural guardian cannot usually sell, mortgage or gift the minor's immovable property without court permission.
minorChildrenRights.account: A minor's share should usually be kept in a separate account in the child's name, operated by a guardian under the law.
minorChildrenRights.majority: Once the child attains majority, they have direct rights over the inherited share.

2.personalLawNote: The Hindu Succession Act applies to Hindus, Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists. Muslims follow personal law; a Will can cover up to one-third of assets. Christians and Parsis follow the Indian Succession Act, and Goa follows the Goa Civil Code. Take legal advice where the family situation is mixed or disputed.

3.title: Restructure and rebuild
3.focus: Secure the family future, update nominations and rebuild stability

0.action: Update nominations on all financial accounts and policies. Most bank accounts can now have up to 4 nominees, depending on the bank and product. {{VERIFY}}
0.why: Up-to-date nominations make this much simpler for your family. This is one of the clearest ways to reduce delay and disputes.

1.action: Draft a Will and, if possible, register it. A registered Will helps your family avoid delays and disputes.
1.why: A Will is useful at any age, especially if you have dependants. It can reduce confusion and make your intentions clear.

2.action: Buy adequate term insurance for earning members. Term insurance replaces lost income so your dependants can manage expenses and future goals.
2.why: This is a straightforward way to protect your family's monthly outgoings and long-term goals.

3.action: Keep health insurance active and review family floater cover. If the deceased had a family floater, tell the insurer to change the proposer before renewal.
3.why: A health policy should not lapse during the transition. Continuity and waiting-period benefits can matter later.

4.action: Build a liquid emergency fund equal to 6 to 12 months of household expenses. Keep it in a savings account or liquid fund rather than locked assets.
4.why: The first 30 days of a crisis are manageable only with accessible cash. Locked investments do not help in an emergency.

5.action: Create an asset register with account numbers, nominees, login details, documents and adviser contacts. Keep one copy in a safe place and one with a trusted family member.
5.why: This is the practical map your family will need if a claim or transfer becomes urgent again.

6.action: Consolidate scattered bank, demat and mutual fund records, and execute a registered Power of Attorney for a trusted person if needed.
6.why: Fewer institutions mean fewer claims, fewer delays and fewer missed assets.
6.legalRef: State power of attorney and financial law

criticalMistakes.1: Investing a large inherited lump sum too quickly while you are still grieving.

criticalMistakes.4: Ignoring tax consequences on sale of inherited assets and not checking the holding structure.
criticalMistakes.5: Thinking a Will is only for older people. A Will is useful at any age, especially if you have dependants.

0.consequence: Waiting periods and continuity benefits may be lost or reset.

1.deadline: No deadline — do it this week.
1.consequence: Without a clear nomination, your family may face a longer and more expensive claim process.

2.deadline: No statutory deadline, but register as soon as possible.
2.consequence: An unregistered Will may still be valid, but it is easier to challenge.

legalHeirCertificate.issuedBy: Tehsildar, revenue authority or municipal corporation
legalHeirCertificate.notSuitableFor: Large bank balances without a nominee or securities above the SEBI threshold

successionCertificate.issuedBy: District Civil Court under Section 372 of the Indian Succession Act
successionCertificate.cost: Court fees usually range from 2% to 3% of the asset value, depending on the state

usedFor.1: Share or demat transmission without a nominee

successionCertificate.notSuitableFor: Immovable property without a Probate or registered Will, depending on the legal position

probate.issuedBy: High Court or District Court, depending on the state and document
probate.mandatory: Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai are mandatory for probate in many cases. Other locations are optional but often strongly recommended.
probate.usedFor: Immovable property transfer based on a Will

irdaiClaimTimeline.standardSettlement: 30 days from receipt of all documents
irdaiClaimTimeline.penaltyForDelay: Interest at bank rate + 2% per year for each day of delay
irdaiClaimTimeline.earlyClaimNote: Early intimation helps the insurer start processing. The 30-day settlement period starts once all documents are submitted.

epfClaimsChecklist.form5IF: EDLI insurance claim — often missed but important

0.definition: The person named to receive certain assets or benefits on death, subject to the legal and account-specific rules.

1.definition: A person entitled to inherit under inheritance law, even if no nominee is named.

2.definition: Updating government land or property records to show the new owner or legal representative.

3.definition: A court process to validate a Will and establish its legal effect.

4.definition: The formal transfer of securities, bank account rights or investment holdings after the holder's death.

5.definition: A legal concept under Hindu succession law that gives co-owners rights in ancestral property.

6.definition: Dying without a valid Will, so inheritance follows the relevant succession law.

7.definition: A charge, mortgage or other burden on property that may affect transfer or sale.

8.definition: A document in which a person agrees to compensate the bank or authority if a claim is later found to be invalid.

9.definition: A person who stands as guarantor or provides assurance for a loan or claim.

10.definition: The record or account number for a mutual fund investment or other securities holding.

11.definition: Depository Participant, the entity that services a demat account.

12.definition: Employee Deposit Linked Insurance, a benefit under EPF that may pay a lump sum to the family on death.

13.definition: A chain of title records showing how a property was inherited or transferred over time.

14.definition: State-specific property or land records used to show ownership, tax status or right to use land.

15.definition: A city historically recognised under the Presidency system, where certain court and probate processes may differ.
